rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A detailed study of Monera reveals the bacterial cell in all its complexity: a capsule, peptidoglycan wall (thick in Gram +ve, thin + LPS in Gram -ve), plasma membrane (with mesosomes in Gram +ve), and cytoplasm containing the naked nucleoid, plasmids, and 70S ribosomes.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Gram -ve: capsule + LPS + thin peptidoglycan + membrane + cytoplasm (70S ribosomes, plasmids, nucleoid)
Gram +ve: capsule + thick peptidoglycan + membrane + mesosomes + cytoplasm
Growth: lag → log (2ⁿ) → stationary → death

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Gram-positive = THICK peptidoglycan (retains crystal violet, purple); Gram-negative = THIN peptidoglycan + outer LPS membrane (stains pink with safranin).  ·  Mesosomes are invaginations of the plasma membrane; they are NOT true organelles (no membrane-bound structure).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB expects detailed Gram + and - bacterium diagrams plus the growth curve.  ·  Gram-staining differentiation (+ve vs -ve) is a very common short-answer.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Gram-negative: E. coli (rod, peritrichous flagella, LPS outer membrane).  ·  Gram-positive: Staphylococcus aureus (coccus, clusters, thick peptidoglycan, mesosomes).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Plasmids are small circular DNA; they are NOT the chromosome (nucleoid).  ·  Endospores are NOT a mode of reproduction; they are survival structures (one endospore → one bacterium).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Bacterial cell = C-W-M-C (Capsule, Wall, Membrane, Cytoplasm).  ·  Gram +ve = thick wall = purple; Gram -ve = thin + LPS = pink.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Bacterial cell: capsule → wall (peptidoglycan) → membrane → cytoplasm (nucleoid, plasmids, 70S ribosomes).  ·  Gram +ve: thick peptidoglycan (purple); Gram -ve: thin + LPS (pink).  ·  Shapes: cocci, bacilli, spirilla, spirochaetes; arrangements: diplo-, strepto-, staphylo-.  ·  Nutrition: autotrophs (photo/chemo) + heterotrophs (saprophytes, parasites).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Bacteria are the oldest and most abundant life form on Earth (~3.5 billion years).  ·  A single E. coli cell can divide in ~20 minutes under optimal conditions.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Explain the bacterial growth curve (4 phases).  ·  Describe the three modes of bacterial genetic exchange.  ·  Explain the role of cyanobacteria in nitrogen fixation.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Cyanobacteria: Nostoc (beaded filaments), Anabaena (heterocysts for N2 fixation), Oscillatoria (trichoid).  ·  Mycoplasma pneumoniae: no wall, pleomorphic, atypical pneumonia.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: DETAILED MONERA (bacterial + cyanobacterial) STRUCTURE AND PHYSIOLOGY.  ·  Bacterial cell (Gram-negative example, E. coli): capsule (slime layer, polysaccharide, virulence) → cell wall (thin peptidoglycan + outer LPS membrane with porins) → plasma membrane (phospholipid + proteins, respiratory + metabolic enzymes) → cytoplasm (70S ribosomes, plasmids, nucleoid).  ·  Bacterial cell (Gram-positive example, Staphylococcus): capsule → thick peptidoglycan cell wall (no outer membrane) → plasma membrane → cytoplasm; mesosomes (invaginations, respiration/secretion).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Bacteria are the simplest, minute, unicellular prokaryotes that can survive even in diverse environments.  ·  Bacteria are found in all possible habitats wherever life can exist.  ·  1 Classification of Kingdom Monera discovered by Dutch naturalist Anton Van Leeuwenhoek in 1675.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The branch of biology that deals with the study of bacteria is called bacteriology.  ·  Bacteria are the smallest of all known cellular organisms.  ·  Key concept 1 for 01 monera general introduction structure of bacterial cell mode of nutrition bacterial growth cyanobacteria virus general introduction structure and importance of virus bacteriophage.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Genetic exchange: conjugation (F+ → F-), transformation (DNA uptake), transduction (phage)  ·  Growth curve: lag, log, stationary, death; generation time (E. coli ~20 min).  ·  Reproduction: binary fission (asexual) + conjugation/transformation/transduction (genetic exchange).
